specStatements.text: This section assumes knowledge of the digestive system studied in Key Stage 3 science.
The digestive system is an example of an organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
Students should be able to relate knowledge of enzymes to Metabolism .
Students should be able to describe the nature of enzyme molecules and relate their activity to temperature and pH changes.
Students should be able to carry out rate calculations for chemical reactions.
Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site.
Students should be able to use the 'lock and key theory' as a simplified model to explain enzyme action.
Students should be able to recall the sites of production and the action of amylase, proteases and lipases.
Students should be able to understand simple word equations but no chemical symbol equations are required.
Digestive enzymes convert food into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates to simple sugars. Amylase is a carbohydrase which breaks down starch.
Proteases break down proteins to amino acids.
Lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.
The products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. Some glucose is used in respiration.

Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It is alkaline to neutralise hydrochloric acid from the stomach. It also emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area. The alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
Students should know the structure and functioning of the human heart and lungs, including how lungs are adapted for gaseous exchange.

The heart is an organ that pumps blood around the body in a double circulatory system. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs where gas exchange takes place. The left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.

Knowledge of the blood vessels associated with the heart is limited to the aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and coronary arteries. Knowledge of the names of the heart valves is not required.
Knowledge of the lungs is restricted to the trachea, bronchi, alveoli and the capillary network surrounding the alveoli.

The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells located in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker. Artificial pacemakers are electrical devices used to correct irregularities in the heart rate.
The body contains three different types of blood vessel: arteries; veins; capillaries.
Students should be able to explain how the structure of these vessels relates to their functions.
Students should be able to use simple compound measures such as rate and carry out rate calculations for blood flow.
Blood is a tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended.
Students should know the functions of each of these blood components.
Students should be able to recognise different types of blood cells in a photograph or diagram, and explain how they are adapted to their functions.
Students should be able to evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of treating cardiovascular diseases by drugs, mechanical devices or transplant.

In coronary heart disease layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them. This reduces the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, resulting in a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle. Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.

In some people heart valves may become faulty, preventing the valve from opening fully, or the heart valve might develop a leak. Students should understand the consequences of faulty valves. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves.

In the case of heart failure a donor heart, or heart and lungs can be transplanted. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.
Students should be able to describe the relationship between health and disease and the interactions between different types of disease.
Health is the state of physical and mental well-being.

Diseases, both communicable Communicable diseases and non-communicable, are major causes of ill health. Other factors including diet, stress and life situations may have a profound effect on both physical and mental health.

Different types of disease may interact. Defects in the immune system mean that an individual is more likely to suffer from infectious diseases.; Viruses living in cells can be the trigger for cancers.; Immune reactions initially caused by a pathogen can trigger allergies such as skin rashes and asthma.; Severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.

Students should be able to translate disease incidence information between graphical and numerical forms, construct and interpret frequency tables and diagrams, bar charts and histograms, and use a scatter diagram to identify a correlation between two variables.
Students should understand the principles of sampling as applied to scientific data, including epidemiological data.

Students should be able to: discuss the human and financial cost of these non-communicable diseases to an individual, a local community, a nation or globally; explain the effect of lifestyle factors including diet, alcohol and smoking on the incidence of non-communicable diseases at local, national and global levels.
Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease.
They can be: aspects of a person's lifestyle; substances in the person's body or environment.

A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others. The effects of diet, smoking and exercise on cardiovascular disease.; Obesity as a risk factor for Type 2 diabetes.; The effect of alcohol on the liver and brain function.; The effect of smoking on lung disease and lung cancer.; The effects of smoking and alcohol on unborn babies.; Carcinogens, including ionising radiation, as risk factors in cancer.
Many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.
Students should be able to understand the principles of sampling as applied to scientific data in terms of risk factors.
Students should be able to translate information between graphical and numerical forms; and extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables in terms of risk factors.
Students should be able to use a scatter diagram to identify a correlation between two variables in terms of risk factors.
Students should be able to describe cancer as the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.
Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane. They do not invade other parts of the body.
Malignant tumour cells are cancers. They invade neighbouring tissues and spread to different parts of the body in the blood where they form secondary tumours.
Scientists have identified lifestyle risk factors for various types of cancer. There are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Key Stage 3 digestion is stated once, as assumed prior knowledge, in concept c41; it is not re-taught and no question assesses it. All other content and every question starts from the digestive system as an organ system and from enzyme action.

Reactions are expressed in words only. Concept c42 gives the word-equation form (for example starch to sugars) and misconception m43 addresses the belief that formulae are required; elsewhere the wording is descriptive, for example starch is broken down to simple sugars and lipids to glycerol and fatty acids. No chemical symbol equation appears in any item.

Only the aorta, vena cava, pulmonary artery, pulmonary vein and coronary arteries are named, in concept c16 and misconception m20. No heart valve is named anywhere in the set; faulty valves are referred to only as 'a heart valve'.
Lung content is limited to the trachea, bronchi, alveoli and the capillary network surrounding the alveoli (concepts c17 and c18, question q12). No other respiratory structure is introduced.

concepts.definition: An organ system in which several organs work together to digest and absorb food.
A large protein molecule that acts as a biological catalyst, speeding up a reaction in a living organism without being changed by it.
The part of an enzyme molecule that the substrate fits into. Its shape means the enzyme catalyses only one specific reaction.
A simplified model of enzyme action in which the substrate (the key) fits into the active site of the enzyme (the lock).
The change in the shape of an enzyme's active site caused by a high temperature or the wrong pH, so that the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.
The sum of all the reactions in a cell or in the body. These reactions are catalysed by enzymes.
The breakdown of food by digestive enzymes into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream.
A carbohydrase is an enzyme that breaks down carbohydrates to simple sugars. Amylase is a carbohydrase which breaks down starch.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins to amino acids.
An enzyme that breaks down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.

concepts.term: Sites of production of digestive enzymes
concepts.definition: Amylase is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine. Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine. Lipase is produced in the pancreas and the small intestine.
The small soluble molecules produced by digestion. They are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.

An alkaline liquid made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It neutralises hydrochloric acid from the stomach and emulsifies fat to form small droplets, which increases the surface area. The alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.
An organ that pumps blood around the body. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, where gas exchange takes place, and the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.
A circulation in which the blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body: once on the way to the lungs and once on the way to the rest of the body.

concepts.term: Blood vessels associated with the heart
concepts.definition: The vena cava carries blood into the heart from the body and the pulmonary artery carries blood from the heart to the lungs. The pulmonary vein carries blood from the lungs back to the heart and the aorta carries blood from the heart to the body. The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle itself.
Air passes down the trachea, into the bronchi and then into the alveoli, which are surrounded by a capillary network.
The tiny air sacs of the lungs, adapted for gaseous exchange by a large surface area, thin walls and the capillary network that surrounds them.
A group of cells located in the right atrium that controls the natural resting heart rate. Artificial pacemakers are electrical devices used to correct irregularities in the heart rate.
A blood vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Its wall is thick, containing muscle and elastic fibres, so that it withstands the high pressure of the blood.
A blood vessel that carries blood back towards the heart. Its wall is thin and it contains valves, because the blood is at low pressure.
A very narrow blood vessel with a wall one cell thick, so that substances can pass quickly between the blood and the tissues.
A tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended.
The liquid part of the blood, which transports the blood cells and dissolved substances around the body.
A blood cell that carries oxygen. It contains haemoglobin, has no nucleus and is a biconcave disc, giving a large surface area for the uptake of oxygen.
A blood cell that defends the body against pathogens, for example by engulfing them or by producing antibodies.
A small fragment of cell suspended in the plasma that helps the blood to clot at a wound.

A disease in which layers of fatty material build up inside the coronary arteries, narrowing them. This reduces the flow of blood through the coronary arteries, resulting in a lack of oxygen for the heart muscle.
Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.
A heart valve that does not open fully, or that develops a leak, so that less blood is pumped or blood flows the wrong way. Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves.

In the case of heart failure a donor heart, or heart and lungs, can be transplanted. Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.
The state of physical and mental well-being.
Communicable diseases can be passed from one person to another, while non-communicable diseases cannot. Both are major causes of ill health.

Different types of disease may interact, for example defects in the immune system make infectious disease more likely, viruses living in cells can trigger cancers, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.
Something that is linked to an increased rate of a disease. Risk factors can be aspects of a person's lifestyle, or substances in the person's body or environment.

An explanation of how a risk factor brings about a disease. A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others, and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.
Choosing a sample that is large enough and representative of the whole population, so that conclusions drawn from scientific data, including epidemiological data, are reliable.
The result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.

Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and do not invade other parts of the body. Malignant tumour cells are cancers: they invade neighbouring tissues and spread to different parts of the body in the blood, where they form secondary tumours.
Lifestyle risk factors have been identified for various types of cancer, and there are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.

Knowledge of the digestive system from Key Stage 3 science is assumed: food passes through the mouth, stomach and small intestine, where it is broken down, and the small soluble products are absorbed in the small intestine.

A reaction written using the names of the substances rather than formulae, for example starch to sugars, or lipids to glycerol and fatty acids. Simple word equations should be understood; no chemical symbol equations are required.

misconceptions.question: What happens to an enzyme molecule after it has catalysed a reaction?
misconceptions.correct: It is unchanged, so it can catalyse the same reaction again.
misconceptions.misconception: Enzymes are used up in the reactions they catalyse.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see the substrate disappear during a reaction and assume the enzyme is consumed with it, as a reactant would be.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site; the enzyme is not changed by the reaction, so a small amount can keep working.

misconceptions.question: An enzyme stops working after being heated to 80 degrees Celsius. Has it been killed?
misconceptions.correct: No. The enzyme is a molecule, not a living thing; the shape of its active site has been changed.
misconceptions.misconception: High temperatures kill enzymes.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'kill' is used for microorganisms harmed by heat, and students transfer it to enzymes because enzymes are made by living cells.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes are protein molecules. Above the optimum temperature the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and the reaction stops.

misconceptions.question: Will an enzyme-controlled reaction keep speeding up as the temperature is raised?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate rises up to an optimum temperature and then falls sharply.
misconceptions.misconception: Raising the temperature always increases the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply the rule they learn for ordinary chemical reactions, where heating increases the rate, without allowing for the shape of the active site.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to relate enzyme activity to temperature changes: above the optimum the active site changes shape, so the rate falls.

misconceptions.question: Do all enzymes work best at pH 7?
misconceptions.correct: No. Different enzymes have different optimum pH values.
misconceptions.misconception: All enzymes work best at pH 7 because that is the pH of the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Neutral pH is treated as 'normal' in chemistry lessons, so students assume every enzyme in the body must need it.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to relate enzyme activity to pH changes: protease in the stomach works in acid conditions, while enzymes in the small intestine work in alkaline conditions.

misconceptions.question: Can one digestive enzyme break down starch, protein and fat?
misconceptions.correct: No. Each enzyme catalyses one specific reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: One digestive enzyme can break down any type of food molecule.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students think of enzymes as a general 'food-breaking' chemical rather than as molecules with a particular shape.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site, so only one type of substrate fits.

misconceptions.question: In the lock and key theory, what fits into what?
misconceptions.correct: The substrate fits into the active site of the enzyme.
misconceptions.misconception: The enzyme changes its shape so that it fits whatever substrate is present.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember that shape matters but not which molecule is fixed, and 'key' and 'lock' get swapped.
misconceptions.correction: In the lock and key theory, used as a simplified model to explain enzyme action, the active site is the lock and the substrate is the key that fits it.

misconceptions.question: Where are digestive enzymes produced?
misconceptions.correct: In several organs, including the salivary glands, the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine.
misconceptions.misconception: All digestive enzymes are made in the stomach.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stomach is the organ students most associate with digestion, so they assume it is where all the chemistry happens.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to recall the sites of production of amylase, proteases and lipases, which include the salivary glands, stomach, pancreas and small intestine.

misconceptions.question: Does bile digest fat?
misconceptions.correct: No. Bile emulsifies fat; lipase digests it.
misconceptions.misconception: Bile is an enzyme that digests fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Bile acts on fat and is released into the small intestine with the digestive enzymes, so students group it with them.
misconceptions.correction: Bile emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area, and the alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase.

misconceptions.question: Which organ makes bile?
misconceptions.correct: The liver makes bile; the gall bladder stores it.
misconceptions.misconception: Bile is made in the gall bladder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The gall bladder is the organ bile is released from, and its name is the one students meet alongside bile.
misconceptions.correction: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder.

misconceptions.question: Does metabolism mean breaking substances down?
misconceptions.correct: No. Metabolism includes reactions that build molecules up as well as reactions that break them down.
misconceptions.misconception: Metabolism means only the breaking down of substances, such as the digestion of food.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet enzymes first in digestion, where large molecules are broken down, and generalise from that example.
misconceptions.correction: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body, and the products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.

misconceptions.question: Are all the products of digestion used for energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are used to build new molecules; only some glucose is used in respiration.
misconceptions.misconception: All the products of digestion are used in respiration to release energy.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Food is described in everyday language as 'fuel', so students assume every digested molecule is burned.
misconceptions.correction: The products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins. Some glucose is used in respiration.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy for a reaction come from when an enzyme speeds it up?
misconceptions.correct: The enzyme does not supply energy; it makes the reaction happen more easily.
misconceptions.misconception: Enzymes supply the energy that reactions need.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link enzymes with speed and speed with energy, so they treat the enzyme as a source of energy.
misconceptions.correction: Enzymes are catalysts that catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site.

misconceptions.question: Is digestion just the breaking of food into smaller pieces?
misconceptions.correct: No. Digestive enzymes change large insoluble molecules into different, smaller soluble molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: Digestion simply breaks food into smaller pieces of the same substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Chewing and the emulsification of fat are physical changes, so students assume the whole process is physical.
misconceptions.correction: Digestive enzymes convert food into small soluble molecules that can be absorbed into the bloodstream, such as simple sugars, amino acids, glycerol and fatty acids.

misconceptions.question: Is all digested food absorbed as glucose?
misconceptions.correct: No. Proteins give amino acids and lipids give glycerol and fatty acids.
misconceptions.misconception: All digested food is absorbed into the blood as glucose.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Glucose is the product students meet most often, because of respiration, so it becomes the default answer for every food group.
misconceptions.correction: Carbohydrases break down carbohydrates to simple sugars, proteases break down proteins to amino acids, and lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids.

misconceptions.question: How is the mean rate of a reaction calculated?
misconceptions.correct: Divide the amount of substance changed by the time taken.
misconceptions.misconception: Rate is found by dividing the time taken by the amount changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recall that rate involves a division but not which quantity goes on top.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to carry out rate calculations for chemical reactions: rate is the amount changed per unit of time.

misconceptions.question: If 20 mg of starch is digested in 5 minutes, is the rate 100 mg per minute?
misconceptions.correct: No. The rate is 20 divided by 5, which is 4 mg per minute.
misconceptions.misconception: Rate is found by multiplying the amount changed by the time taken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see two numbers in a rate question and combine them with the operation that gives the larger, more impressive answer.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to carry out rate calculations for chemical reactions: divide the amount changed by the time taken.

misconceptions.question: Is the rate of blood flow the same as the total volume of blood pumped?
misconceptions.correct: No. A rate must state the volume for each unit of time.
misconceptions.misconception: The rate is the total amount changed, whatever the time taken.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students quote the number given in the question because it is the only volume they can see.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to use simple compound measures such as rate and carry out rate calculations for blood flow, giving the volume per unit of time.

misconceptions.question: Which ventricle pumps blood to the lungs?
misconceptions.correct: The right ventricle.
misconceptions.misconception: The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams of the heart are drawn as though facing the patient, so the right side of the heart appears on the left of the page.
misconceptions.correction: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs where gas exchange takes place. The left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.

misconceptions.question: How many times does blood pass through the heart in one complete circuit of the body?
misconceptions.correct: Twice: once to the lungs and once to the rest of the body.
misconceptions.misconception: Blood passes through the heart once in each complete circuit of the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture the circulation as a single loop, which is what a diagram of one artery and one vein suggests.
misconceptions.correction: The heart pumps blood around the body in a double circulatory system.

misconceptions.question: Do all arteries carry oxygenated blood?
misconceptions.correct: No. The pulmonary artery carries blood to the lungs for gas exchange.
misconceptions.misconception: All arteries carry blood that is rich in oxygen.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn the useful rule that arteries carry blood away from the heart and then attach oxygen to it because most arteries do carry oxygenated blood.
misconceptions.correction: Knowledge of the blood vessels associated with the heart includes the pulmonary artery, which carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs where gas exchange takes place.

misconceptions.question: Do veins have thick muscular walls?
misconceptions.correct: No. Veins have thin walls, because the blood in them is at low pressure.
misconceptions.misconception: Veins have thick muscular walls like arteries.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Veins look wide and obvious under the skin, so students assume they must be strongly built.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to explain how the structure of the vessels relates to their functions: an artery has a thick wall to withstand high pressure, while a vein has a thin wall and valves.

misconceptions.question: Why is the wall of a capillary only one cell thick?
misconceptions.correct: So that substances can pass quickly between the blood and the tissues.
misconceptions.misconception: Capillaries have thick walls so that they can withstand the pressure of the blood.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students apply the artery rule, that a strong wall resists pressure, to every vessel instead of matching structure to function.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to explain how the structure of these vessels relates to their functions: the capillary wall is one cell thick to allow exchange.

misconceptions.question: Where in the lungs does gas exchange take place?
misconceptions.correct: In the alveoli, which are surrounded by a capillary network.
misconceptions.misconception: Gas exchange takes place in the trachea and the bronchi.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The trachea and bronchi are the largest and most obvious structures on a diagram, so students assume the important work happens there.
misconceptions.correction: Knowledge of the lungs is restricted to the trachea, bronchi, alveoli and the capillary network surrounding the alveoli; the alveoli are where gaseous exchange occurs.

misconceptions.question: Do red blood cells have a nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: No. They have no nucleus, which leaves more room for haemoglobin.
misconceptions.misconception: Red blood cells contain a nucleus like other animal cells.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that animal cells have a nucleus and apply the rule to every cell they are shown.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to recognise different types of blood cell in a photograph or diagram and explain how they are adapted to their functions: a red blood cell has no nucleus.

misconceptions.question: What do platelets do?
misconceptions.correct: They help the blood to clot at a wound.
misconceptions.misconception: Platelets destroy pathogens that enter the blood.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Platelets are small fragments that look like cells in a photograph, so students confuse them with white blood cells.
misconceptions.correction: Blood consists of plasma, in which the red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets are suspended: white blood cells defend against pathogens and platelets help clotting.

misconceptions.question: Which part of the blood carries oxygen?
misconceptions.correct: The red blood cells, because they contain haemoglobin.
misconceptions.misconception: Plasma carries the oxygen around the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Plasma is described as the transport liquid of the blood, so students assume it carries everything, including oxygen.
misconceptions.correction: Blood is a tissue consisting of plasma, in which the red blood cells are suspended; the red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen.

misconceptions.question: What do statins do to a narrowed coronary artery?
misconceptions.correct: They reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.
misconceptions.misconception: Statins widen the narrowed coronary arteries.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Statins and stents are taught together as treatments for the same disease and their names sound alike.
misconceptions.correction: Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open. Statins are widely used to reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows down the rate of fatty material deposit.

misconceptions.question: Do stents lower the level of cholesterol in the blood?
misconceptions.correct: No. A stent is a device that holds the artery open.
misconceptions.misconception: Stents lower the level of cholesterol in the blood.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both stents and statins are used for coronary heart disease, so students swap the mechanical device and the drug.
misconceptions.correction: Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open, while statins are used to reduce blood cholesterol levels.

misconceptions.question: A heart valve develops a leak. Does this affect how much blood is pumped?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Blood flows back the wrong way, so less blood is pumped to the body.
misconceptions.misconception: A leaking heart valve does not change the volume of blood the heart pumps out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The heart keeps beating and the person often feels well at first, so students assume nothing has changed.
misconceptions.correction: In some people heart valves may become faulty, preventing the valve from opening fully, or the heart valve might develop a leak; students should understand the consequences of faulty valves.

misconceptions.question: Is an artificial heart a permanent replacement for a diseased heart?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is used while a patient waits for a transplant, or to allow the heart to rest.
misconceptions.misconception: An artificial heart is a permanent cure for heart failure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'artificial heart' suggests a complete replacement organ, like an artificial limb.
misconceptions.correction: Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.

misconceptions.question: Does health mean being free from disease?
misconceptions.correct: No. Health is the state of physical and mental well-being.
misconceptions.misconception: Health means simply being free from disease.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Health is usually discussed in the context of illness, so students define it as the absence of illness rather than as well-being.
misconceptions.correction: Health is the state of physical and mental well-being, and other factors including diet, stress and life situations may have a profound effect on both physical and mental health.

misconceptions.question: Can one type of disease make another type more likely?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Different types of disease may interact.
misconceptions.misconception: Different types of disease cannot affect one another.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diseases are taught in separate categories, so students treat communicable disease, cancer, allergy and mental illness as unconnected.
misconceptions.correction: Different types of disease may interact: defects in the immune system mean an individual is more likely to suffer from infectious diseases, viruses living in cells can be the trigger for cancers, immune reactions initially caused by a pathogen can trigger allergies, and severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.

misconceptions.question: A scatter diagram shows a correlation between two variables. Does this prove that one causes the other?
misconceptions.correct: No. A correlation shows the two are linked; further evidence is needed to prove a causal mechanism.
misconceptions.misconception: A correlation between two variables proves that one of them causes the other.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Graphs feel like proof, and students are taught to describe a pattern before they are taught what a pattern can and cannot show.
misconceptions.correction: A causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors, but not in others; students should use a scatter diagram to identify a correlation between two variables.

misconceptions.question: If someone is exposed to a risk factor, will they get the disease?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. The risk factor increases the rate of the disease in a population.
misconceptions.misconception: A risk factor will cause the disease in everyone who is exposed to it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'factor' sounds like a cause, and students know one person who was affected, so they read a population statement as a personal certainty.
misconceptions.correction: Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease, and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.

misconceptions.question: Is a study of 20 people enough to show that a substance is a risk factor?
misconceptions.correct: No. The sample is too small to represent the population reliably.
misconceptions.misconception: A small sample gives results that are as reliable as those from a large sample.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge data by whether it shows a clear pattern rather than by how it was collected.
misconceptions.correction: Students should understand the principles of sampling as applied to scientific data, including epidemiological data.

misconceptions.question: Do benign tumours spread to other parts of the body?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are contained in one area and do not invade other parts of the body.
misconceptions.misconception: Benign tumours invade neighbouring tissues and spread around the body.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any tumour sounds dangerous, so students treat 'benign' and 'malignant' as two words for the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Benign tumours are growths of abnormal cells which are contained in one area, usually within a membrane, and they do not invade other parts of the body.

misconceptions.question: Are all cancers caused by lifestyle?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.
misconceptions.misconception: All cancers are caused by lifestyle factors such as smoking and diet.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Public health campaigns concentrate on lifestyle, so students assume every case must have a lifestyle cause.
misconceptions.correction: Scientists have identified lifestyle risk factors for various types of cancer. There are also genetic risk factors for some cancers.

misconceptions.question: What is happening to cells in a tumour?
misconceptions.correct: They are growing and dividing in an uncontrolled way.
misconceptions.misconception: Cancer is the result of cells dying rather than dividing uncontrollably.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Cancer is associated with damage and death, so students assume the cells themselves are dying.
misconceptions.correction: Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.

misconceptions.question: Which blood vessels contain valves?
misconceptions.correct: Veins contain valves; arteries do not.
misconceptions.misconception: Arteries contain valves to stop the blood flowing backwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Valves are taught as the structure that keeps blood moving one way, so students give them to the vessel they think of as most important.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to explain how the structure of these vessels relates to their functions: valves are found in veins, where the blood is at low pressure.

misconceptions.question: How can a faulty heart valve be treated?
misconceptions.correct: It can be replaced with a biological or a mechanical valve.
misconceptions.misconception: A faulty heart valve can only be treated by a heart transplant.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Valves are part of the heart, so students assume the whole organ has to be replaced.
misconceptions.correction: Faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves; a donor heart is transplanted in the case of heart failure.

misconceptions.question: Who bears the cost of non-communicable disease?
misconceptions.correct: The individual, and also the local community, the nation and the world.
misconceptions.misconception: Non-communicable disease costs affect only the person who is ill.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Non-communicable diseases cannot be passed on, so students assume their effects stop with the patient.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to discuss the human and financial cost of these non-communicable diseases to an individual, a local community, a nation or globally.

misconceptions.question: Where are the pacemaker cells found?
misconceptions.correct: In the right atrium of the heart.
misconceptions.misconception: The cells that set the resting heart rate are found in the left ventricle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The left ventricle has the thickest muscle, so students assume it must be in charge of the beat.
misconceptions.correction: The natural resting heart rate is controlled by a group of cells located in the right atrium that act as a pacemaker.

misconceptions.question: How should the breakdown of starch by amylase be written?
misconceptions.correct: As a simple word equation, using the names of the substances: starch to sugars.
misconceptions.misconception: Digestion reactions have to be written as chemical symbol equations.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry over the symbol equations and formulae they meet in chemistry lessons and assume the same is expected of them in biology.
misconceptions.correction: Students should be able to understand simple word equations, but no chemical symbol equations are required in this topic.

mcqs.stem: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions. What causes this specificity?

options.text: The temperature at which the enzyme works.
options.rationale: A student who believes that raising the temperature always speeds an enzyme up treats temperature as the property that decides what the enzyme does; temperature changes the rate, not which reaction is catalysed.

options.text: The shape of the enzyme's active site.
options.rationale: Enzymes catalyse specific reactions in living organisms due to the shape of their active site, which only one substrate fits.

options.text: The amount of the enzyme that is used.
options.rationale: A student who thinks enzymes are used up sees the quantity of enzyme as the key variable; the amount affects how fast the reaction goes, not which substrate fits the active site.

options.text: The pH at which the enzyme is stored.
options.rationale: A student who believes every enzyme needs pH 7 focuses on pH as the controlling factor; pH affects the shape of the active site but does not decide which reaction the enzyme catalyses.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the lock and key theory of enzyme action?

options.text: The enzyme fits into every kind of substrate.
options.rationale: A student who thinks one enzyme digests all foods expects it to fit every substrate; enzymes catalyse specific reactions due to the shape of their active site.

options.text: The enzyme is used up by its own substrate.
options.rationale: A student who believes enzymes are consumed reads the model as the substrate destroying the lock; the enzyme is a catalyst and is unchanged by the reaction.

options.text: The enzyme changes shape to fit any substrate.
options.rationale: A student who has the lock and key the wrong way round thinks the enzyme moulds itself; the active site has a fixed shape that only one substrate fits.

options.text: The substrate fits the enzyme's active site.
options.rationale: In the lock and key theory, used as a simplified model of enzyme action, the substrate is the key that fits the active site of the enzyme.

mcqs.stem: An enzyme-controlled reaction is fastest at 40 degrees Celsius. What happens at 60 degrees Celsius?

options.text: The rate falls because the enzyme has been killed.
options.rationale: A student who thinks of enzymes as alive uses 'killed' for what heat does; an enzyme is a protein molecule and its active site changes shape.

options.text: The rate falls because the enzyme is used up.
options.rationale: A student who believes enzymes are consumed blames the fall on the enzyme running out; enzymes are catalysts and are not changed by the reaction.

options.text: The rate rises because the enzyme works faster.
options.rationale: A student who believes heating always speeds a reaction up applies the rule beyond the optimum; past the optimum the active site changes shape and the rate falls.

options.text: The rate falls because the active site changes shape.
options.rationale: Above the optimum temperature the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and the rate falls.

mcqs.stem: Protease in the stomach works fastest at pH 2. What happens to its activity at pH 8?

options.text: It falls, as the active site changes shape.
options.rationale: Away from its optimum pH the shape of the active site changes, so the substrate no longer fits and activity falls.

options.text: It rises, as enzymes work best at about pH 7.
options.rationale: A student who believes all enzymes prefer neutral conditions expects pH 8 to suit this enzyme; different enzymes have different optimum pH values and this one works in acid.

options.text: It falls, as the enzyme is killed by alkali.
options.rationale: A student who treats enzymes as living things says alkali kills them; the enzyme is a molecule whose active site changes shape.

options.text: It falls, as the enzyme has been used up.
options.rationale: A student who believes enzymes are consumed blames the fall on the enzyme running out; the change in pH has altered the shape of the active site.

mcqs.stem: Amylase broke down 20 mg of starch in 5 minutes. What was the mean rate of reaction?

options.text: 4 mg per minute
options.rationale: The mean rate is the amount changed divided by the time taken: 20 mg divided by 5 minutes.

options.text: 0.25 mg per minute
options.rationale: A student who divides the time by the amount gets 5 divided by 20; rate is the amount changed per unit of time.

options.text: 20 mg per minute
options.rationale: A student who quotes the total mass changed ignores the time taken; a rate must state the amount for each minute.

options.text: 100 mg per minute
options.rationale: A student who multiplies the amount by the time gets 20 times 5; the two quantities must be divided, not multiplied.

mcqs.stem: Enzymes are involved in metabolism. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Enzymes catalyse the reactions of metabolism in cells.
options.rationale: Metabolism is the sum of all the reactions in a cell or the body, and each of those reactions is catalysed by an enzyme.

options.text: Enzymes give the reactions the energy that they need.
options.rationale: A student who links enzymes with speed assumes they supply energy; an enzyme is a catalyst and does not provide energy.

options.text: Enzymes are used up in the reactions that they speed up.
options.rationale: A student who treats the enzyme as a reactant expects it to be consumed; an enzyme is a catalyst and is unchanged by the reaction.

options.text: Enzymes catalyse only reactions that break down food.
options.rationale: A student who first meets enzymes in digestion assumes metabolism is only breakdown; the products of digestion are also built up into new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about digestive enzymes is correct?

options.text: Bile is the enzyme that breaks down fat droplets.
options.rationale: A student who sees bile acting on fat classes it as an enzyme; bile emulsifies fat to increase the surface area, and lipase breaks the fat down.

options.text: One enzyme is able to digest every type of food.
options.rationale: A student who thinks of enzymes as general food-breakers expects one to do all the work; each enzyme catalyses a specific reaction because of the shape of its active site.

options.text: Protease is made in the stomach and pancreas.
options.rationale: Protease is produced in the stomach, the pancreas and the small intestine, and it breaks down proteins to amino acids.

options.text: Amylase is made only in the wall of the stomach.
options.rationale: A student who thinks all digestion is stomach chemistry places every enzyme there; amylase is produced in the salivary glands, the pancreas and the small intestine.

mcqs.stem: What does lipase break lipids down into?

options.text: Glucose and fatty acids
options.rationale: A student who thinks all digested food becomes glucose replaces glycerol with it; lipids give glycerol and fatty acids, while carbohydrates give simple sugars.

options.text: Glycerol and fatty acids
options.rationale: Lipases break down lipids (fats) to glycerol and fatty acids, which are small soluble molecules that can be absorbed.

options.text: Amino acids and simple sugars
options.rationale: A student who does not link each enzyme to a specific substrate mixes the products of protein and carbohydrate digestion; those come from proteases and carbohydrases.

options.text: Small droplets of lipid
options.rationale: A student who thinks digestion only makes pieces smaller describes emulsification; small droplets are still lipid, and lipase changes them chemically.

mcqs.stem: Why does bile increase the rate of fat breakdown by lipase?

options.text: It digests the fat into fatty acids and glycerol.
options.rationale: A student who classes bile as an enzyme credits it with the chemical breakdown; bile only emulsifies the fat, and lipase digests it.

options.text: It gives the lipase the energy that it needs.
options.rationale: A student who thinks enzymes need an energy supply casts bile in that role; bile works by increasing surface area and making conditions alkaline.

options.text: It emulsifies fat, so surface area increases.
options.rationale: Bile emulsifies fat to form small droplets which increases the surface area, and the alkaline conditions and large surface area increase the rate of breakdown by lipase.

options.text: It makes the small intestine neutral at pH 7.
options.rationale: A student who believes every enzyme needs pH 7 assumes bile neutralises to exactly that; bile is alkaline and creates alkaline conditions that suit lipase.

mcqs.stem: What happens to the products of digestion after they are absorbed?

options.text: Every product is turned into glucose and stored.
options.rationale: A student who thinks every product becomes glucose gives one fate to all three food groups; amino acids and fatty acids are used to build proteins and lipids.

options.text: They are all used in respiration to give energy.
options.rationale: A student who thinks of food only as fuel sends every product to respiration; only some of the glucose is respired and the rest is used for building.

options.text: They build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins.
options.rationale: The products of digestion are used to build new carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and some glucose is used in respiration.

options.text: They join back to form the first food molecules.
options.rationale: A student who sees digestion as a physical change expects the original molecules to reappear; the products are used to build new molecules the body needs.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the double circulatory system is correct?

options.text: Blood passes through the heart once each circuit.
options.rationale: A student who pictures a single loop counts one pass; in a double circulatory system the blood passes through the heart twice in each circuit.

options.text: Arteries carry blood with oxygen to the lungs.
options.rationale: A student who believes every artery carries oxygenated blood misreads the pulmonary artery; it carries blood to the lungs, where gas exchange takes place.

options.text: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
options.rationale: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs where gas exchange takes place, while the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.

options.text: The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs.
options.rationale: A student who reads a heart diagram as though it were their own left and right swaps the two sides; the left ventricle pumps blood around the rest of the body.

mcqs.stem: Which feature of the alveoli increases the rate of gaseous exchange?

options.text: A wide tube that carries air down to the lungs.
options.rationale: A student who thinks exchange happens in the airways describes the trachea; gaseous exchange takes place in the alveoli, not in the trachea or bronchi.

options.text: A thick outer wall that resists air pressure.
options.rationale: A student who assumes thick walls are always an advantage applies the artery rule; the alveolus wall is thin so that gases pass through quickly.

options.text: A supply of plasma that takes up the oxygen.
options.rationale: A student who thinks plasma carries oxygen looks for it at the exchange surface; oxygen is carried by the red blood cells in the capillary network.

options.text: A large surface area and a good blood supply.
options.rationale: The alveoli are adapted for gaseous exchange by a large surface area and the capillary network that surrounds them.

mcqs.stem: Which pairing of a blood vessel with its structure is correct?

options.text: Artery: thick wall resists the high pressure.
options.rationale: An artery carries blood away from the heart at high pressure, so its wall is thick, with muscle and elastic fibres.

options.text: Vein: thick muscular wall resists high pressure.
options.rationale: A student who treats all vessels as alike gives the vein an artery's wall; blood in a vein is at low pressure, so the wall is thin.

options.text: Capillary: thick wall resists the blood pressure.
options.rationale: A student who assumes a strong wall is always useful ignores the capillary's job; its wall is one cell thick so substances can pass through quickly.

options.text: Artery: valves stop blood flowing backwards.
options.rationale: A student who remembers valves keep blood moving one way puts them in the main vessel; valves are found in veins, where the pressure is low.

mcqs.stem: A heart pumps 300 cm3 of blood in 4 seconds. What is the rate of blood flow?

options.text: 1200 cm3 per second
options.rationale: A student who multiplies the volume by the time gets 300 times 4; the two quantities must be divided.

options.text: 75 cm3 per second
options.rationale: Rate of blood flow is the volume divided by the time taken: 300 cm3 divided by 4 seconds.

options.text: 300 cm3 per second
options.rationale: A student who quotes the total volume ignores the time taken; a rate must give the volume for each second.

options.text: 0.01 cm3 per second
options.rationale: A student who divides the time by the volume gets 4 divided by 300; the volume must be divided by the time.

mcqs.stem: A photograph shows the cells in a sample of blood. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Platelets move around the blood and destroy pathogens.
options.rationale: A student who sees small fragments in a photograph confuses platelets with white blood cells; platelets help the blood to clot.

options.text: Plasma is the liquid that carries oxygen to the cells.
options.rationale: A student who knows plasma is the transport liquid assumes it carries oxygen too; oxygen is carried by the red blood cells.

options.text: Red blood cells have a nucleus that controls oxygen use.
options.rationale: A student who applies the rule that animal cells have a nucleus adds one to the red blood cell; the mature red blood cell has none.

options.text: Red blood cells have no nucleus, so they carry more oxygen.
options.rationale: A red blood cell is adapted to its function of carrying oxygen: it has no nucleus, leaving more room for haemoglobin.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the treatment of coronary heart disease is correct?

options.text: Statins are used to widen the blocked coronary arteries.
options.rationale: A student who confuses the drug with the device gives statins a mechanical job; statins reduce blood cholesterol levels, which slows the rate of fatty deposit.

options.text: Stents are used to keep the coronary arteries open.
options.rationale: In coronary heart disease fatty material narrows the coronary arteries, and stents are used to keep them open.

options.text: Stents are used to lower the level of blood cholesterol.
options.rationale: A student who swaps the two treatments gives the device the drug's action; a stent physically holds the artery open.

options.text: Artificial hearts are used to cure the heart disease.
options.rationale: A student who sees an artificial heart as a replacement organ treats it as a cure; it keeps a patient alive whilst waiting for a transplant or lets the heart rest.

mcqs.stem: A person has a heart valve that has developed a leak. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Blood flows backwards through the leaking valve.
options.rationale: A faulty valve that leaks lets blood flow backwards, so less blood is pumped forward to the body.

options.text: The volume of blood pumped stays the same.
options.rationale: A student who sees the heart still beating assumes nothing has changed; blood leaking backwards reduces the volume pumped on each beat.

options.text: Only a heart transplant can treat the problem.
options.rationale: A student who thinks the whole organ must be replaced overlooks valve surgery; faulty heart valves can be replaced using biological or mechanical valves.

options.text: An artificial heart gives a permanent cure.
options.rationale: A student who treats an artificial heart as a replacement organ offers it as a cure; it is used while waiting for a transplant or to allow the heart to rest.

mcqs.stem: Why might an artificial heart be used for a patient with heart failure?

options.text: It keeps a patient alive while awaiting a donor.
options.rationale: Artificial hearts are occasionally used to keep patients alive whilst waiting for a heart transplant, or to allow the heart to rest as an aid to recovery.

options.text: It replaces a faulty valve inside the patient.
options.rationale: A student who does not separate valve disease from heart failure blurs the two treatments; faulty valves are replaced with biological or mechanical valves.

options.text: It cures the heart failure without any further care.
options.rationale: A student who reads 'artificial heart' as a replacement organ expects a permanent cure; it is a temporary measure while a donor heart is awaited.

options.text: It lowers the level of cholesterol in the blood.
options.rationale: A student who mixes up the treatments gives the device the action of a statin; only statins reduce blood cholesterol levels.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes health?

options.text: The state of being free of catching diseases.
options.rationale: A student who thinks only about communicable disease ignores non-communicable disease and mental health, both of which affect health.

options.text: The state of having no risk factors present.
options.rationale: A student who treats a risk factor as a certain cause equates health with avoiding them; risk factors are linked to an increased rate of disease, not to the definition of health.

options.text: The state of both physical and mental well-being.
options.rationale: Health is the state of physical and mental well-being, so it is more than the absence of disease.

options.text: The state of the body when disease is absent.
options.rationale: A student who defines health by illness leaves out well-being; health is the state of physical and mental well-being.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the interaction of different types of disease is correct?

options.text: Communicable disease has no effect on other illness.
options.rationale: A student who keeps the categories of disease separate rules out any link; defects in the immune system, for example, make infectious disease more likely.

options.text: Mental illness is not affected by physical illness.
options.rationale: A student whose definition of health leaves out mental well-being separates the two; severe physical ill health can lead to depression and other mental illness.

options.text: Cancers are triggered by lifestyle, not by viruses.
options.rationale: A student who thinks cancer is purely a lifestyle disease rejects other triggers; viruses living in cells can be the trigger for cancers.

options.text: An immune reaction to a pathogen can trigger allergies.
options.rationale: Different types of disease may interact: immune reactions initially caused by a pathogen can trigger allergies such as skin rashes and asthma.

mcqs.stem: A scatter diagram shows a correlation between hours of exercise and heart health. What can be concluded?

options.text: Exercise has been proved to cause good heart health.
options.rationale: A student who reads a graph as proof jumps from correlation to cause; further evidence is needed before a causal mechanism is established.

options.text: People who exercise avoid getting heart disease.
options.rationale: A student who treats a risk factor as certain applies a population trend to every individual; risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease.

options.text: The variables are linked, but no cause is proven.
options.rationale: A scatter diagram can be used to identify a correlation between two variables, but a causal mechanism has been proven for some risk factors and not for others.

options.text: The sample size does not matter for this result.
options.rationale: A student who judges data by its pattern alone ignores how it was collected; a sample must be large enough and representative to be reliable.

mcqs.stem: A scientist studies whether a substance is a risk factor using data from 20 people. Why is this a problem?

options.text: A risk factor affects each person in the sample.
options.rationale: A student who treats a risk factor as a certain cause expects it to show in everyone; risk factors are linked to an increased rate of disease in a population.

options.text: The sample size has no effect on the result.
options.rationale: A student who thinks any sample will do sees no problem; a small sample may not represent the population, so the conclusion is unreliable.

options.text: A correlation in the data would prove a cause.
options.rationale: A student who equates correlation with cause thinks the study design does not matter; a correlation shows a link, and a causal mechanism must be proven separately.

options.text: The sample is too small to be representative.
options.rationale: The principles of sampling applied to epidemiological data require a sample large enough to represent the population before conclusions are drawn.

mcqs.stem: Smoking is described as a risk factor for lung cancer. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A correlation in data proves that it is a cause.
options.rationale: A student who reads a correlation as proof stops at the graph; a causal mechanism has been proven for smoking by further evidence, not by correlation alone.

options.text: It is a factor linked to an increased rate of disease.
options.rationale: Risk factors are linked to an increased rate of a disease, and smoking is a lifestyle risk factor for lung disease and lung cancer.

options.text: It is the one risk factor for this type of cancer.
options.rationale: A student who thinks cancer is only a lifestyle disease overlooks other factors; there are also genetic risk factors and many diseases are caused by the interaction of a number of factors.

options.text: It leads to the disease in each person who smokes.
options.rationale: A student who treats a risk factor as a certain cause applies it to every individual; the link is to an increased rate of the disease in a population.

mcqs.stem: What is happening to the cells in a tumour?

options.text: Changes in cells lead to uncontrolled growth.
options.rationale: Cancer is the result of changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.

options.text: The cells in the tissue die and are not replaced.
options.rationale: A student who links cancer with damage assumes the cells are dying; the cells are growing and dividing in an uncontrolled way.

options.text: Benign cells travel around in the bloodstream.
options.rationale: A student who treats all tumours as the same has benign cells spreading; benign tumours are contained in one area and do not invade other parts of the body.

options.text: Lifestyle damages the membrane around the cell.
options.rationale: A student who thinks lifestyle is the whole story describes a lifestyle mechanism; cancer results from changes in cells, and there are genetic risk factors as well.

mcqs.stem: How do malignant tumour cells differ from benign tumour cells?

options.text: They stay inside a membrane in one part of the body.
options.rationale: A student who does not separate the two types describes a benign tumour; it is the benign tumour that is contained in one area within a membrane.

options.text: They invade tissues and form secondary tumours.
options.rationale: Malignant tumour cells are cancers: they invade neighbouring tissues and spread in the blood to different parts of the body, where they form secondary tumours.

options.text: They are caused by lifestyle rather than by genes.
options.rationale: A student who thinks all cancer is a lifestyle disease uses cause to tell the types apart; there are also genetic risk factors, and the difference is whether cells spread.

options.text: They divide more slowly than normal healthy cells.
options.rationale: A student who pictures cancer as cells failing assumes slower division; cancer results from changes that lead to uncontrolled growth and division.
